lines: The exact same order, kept two different ways.
One keeps a single row for the whole thing. The other keeps one row per line inside it. Ask which product actually sold, and only one of them can even answer.
Four decisions, always made in the same order.
What business process. What one row of the result represents. What it's broken down by. And what's actually being measured.
That second decision is the one everything else depends on.
Deciding what a single row represents has to happen before anything else, because every later choice has to agree with it.
Here's where that gets decided for real.
An order and its line items need one fact table. Should one row be the whole order, or just one of its lines?
answer: One of its lines. That's the most basic unit this process actually produces.
The order itself is really just several of those added together.

lines: Here's the proof, run for real.
Add up every line's own total, grouped however you like, and you land back on the exact order total every single time.
Now, here's what the other choice would actually have cost you.
A table kept at one row per whole order never had a column for which product, or how many, in the first place. Not a harder question. One it simply has no way to answer.
Here's the first kind, of three you'll run into.
This one adds up correctly no matter how you slice it, and that was just checked directly, not assumed.
Here's the second kind, tested the same way.
A balance adds up fine across different accounts. Does it add up the same way across different stretches of time for the same account?
answer: No. Adding up several time periods' balances gives you a number that means nothing at all.
The real year-end figure is just whatever the last period's own balance happened to be.

lines: Watch that happen with real numbers.
Four quarters' balances, added together, land on a total with no meaning. The actual year-end balance was simply the fourth quarter's own number, sitting there the whole time.
Now the third kind, and this one can't be added up at all, not even halfway.
Average two regions' profit margins the obvious way, and you get a different answer than if you add up their revenue and their cost separately first, and only then divide.
Here's the actual fix, and it's simpler than it sounds.
Keep the pieces that do add up safely. Add those. Only compute the ratio at the very end, after the adding is already done.
Four decisions, in order, with the second one binding everything after it.
One kind of number adds up anywhere. One adds up almost anywhere, except across time. One doesn't add up at all, only its pieces do.
Last one. A shipping cost, divided by how many units shipped.
Is it safe to just add that number up across orders, or does it need the same fix as the profit margin did?
answer: The same fix. Add up the shipping cost and the unit count separately, then divide once at the end.
It's a ratio for exactly the same reason the margin was, so it breaks the same way if you add it up directly.
